title: Workshop Safety
intro: Brake work involves heavy vehicles, hazardous dust and chemicals, and parts that determine whether a vehicle can stop. Safe habits come first. This chapter covers protective equipment, lifting, chemical handling, housekeeping and environmental care.
objectives: List and explain personal protective equipment (PPE) for brake work.
Describe the correct way to lift and support a vehicle.
Explain safe handling of brake fluid, brake dust and other chemicals.
Describe good housekeeping and correct waste disposal.

r: Protect eyes from brake fluid splashes, springs, dust and debris.
Wear them whenever working under a vehicle or cleaning parts.
Protect skin from brake fluid, cleaners, hot parts and sharp edges.
Use chemical-resistant gloves (such as nitrile) for fluid and cleaners.
Protects feet from dropped parts and the vehicle's weight.
Closed, sturdy shoes with non-slip soles; steel or composite toe.
Keep fluid and dust off skin and clothes.
Avoid loose clothing or jewellery near moving parts.
Reduces breathing of dust where dust cannot be avoided.
Use equipment rated for fine dust. Do not rely on a mask as the only control.
Protects against noisy tools such as air tools.

blocks: Follow the sequence from Chapter 4: level ground, parking brake and transmission set, wheel chocks, jack at the lift point, **jack stands** under approved support points, and a gentle shake test before working.

ul: Never use bricks, wood blocks or concrete blocks as supports.
Never put any part of your body under a vehicle that is on a jack only.
Do not run the engine with the vehicle on stands unless a procedure requires it and the vehicle is secured.
When lowering the vehicle, make sure that tools and people are clear.

blocks.warn: Vehicles fall suddenly and without warning. Treat every raised vehicle as dangerous until it is supported by stands and chocked.

ul: Brake fluid can **irritate skin and eyes**. Wear gloves and eye protection. If it touches skin, wash with soap and water. For eyes, rinse with water for several minutes and seek medical attention.
Most brake fluids **damage paint**. Cover painted surfaces and wipe up spills immediately with water.
Keep containers **closed**; glycol-based fluid absorbs moisture from the air.
Use **fresh fluid** from a sealed container, and never use fluid that has been left open or that was drained from the system.
Use only the fluid type specified by the manufacturer.
Keep fluid away from children and animals; it is toxic if swallowed.

blocks: Brake dust is fine particulate that should not be breathed. Older or imported friction materials may contain hazardous materials, and the contents cannot be known by looking at it. **Treat all brake dust as hazardous.**

ul: **Never blow dust off with compressed air.** This puts dust in the air.
Use an **enclosed brake washer, a vacuum designed for fine dust (HEPA), or a wet cleaning method** approved for your workplace.
Do not dry-brush or dry-sweep brake dust.
Wash hands and face before eating, drinking or smoking.
Do not take dusty work clothes home; launder them separately.

blocks: Brake cleaners, solvents, penetrating oils, lubricants and fluids are all chemicals. Before using one:

ol: Read the **label and safety data sheet** for hazards.
Keep away from **flames, sparks and hot surfaces** because many cleaners are flammable.
Never put chemicals in drink bottles.

blocks.warn: Some brake cleaners can produce harmful fumes if exposed to heat, such as welding, hot surfaces or open flames. Keep them away from heat sources.

ul: Keep floors **clean and dry**. Wipe up fluid spills immediately.
Keep walkways clear of hoses, cords and tools.
Return tools to their storage after use.
Keep a fire extinguisher accessible and know how to use it.
Keep a first aid kit and eye wash available.
Keep lighting good, especially under the vehicle.
Tag a vehicle that is unsafe or under repair.
Collect used **brake fluid** in a labelled, sealed container. Do not pour it on the ground or down drains.
Dispose of used fluid, contaminated rags, cleaners, and brake dust waste **according to local regulations**, using approved collection points.
Used pads, shoes and rotors may be recycled in some places; follow local rules.
Use drip pans and absorbent materials to prevent spills.
Close containers after use and store waste safely until collected.

blocks: Brake fluid and cleaning chemicals can contaminate soil and water. Careful disposal protects the people and the environment around you.

check.title: Workshop Safety Checklist
items: Gloves are worn and in good condition.
Loose clothing, jewellery and long hair are secured.
The work area is level, clean and dry.
The vehicle is chocked, with the parking brake and transmission set.
The vehicle is lifted at the correct points and supported on jack stands.
No one is under a vehicle on a jack only.
Brake fluid is in a sealed container and spills are cleaned up.
No compressed air is used to blow brake dust.
Fire extinguisher, first aid kit and eye wash are accessible.
Waste containers are available for fluid, rags and dust waste.

concepts: PPE is the last line of defence, but it must always be used.
Jack stands, not jacks, hold the vehicle up.
Brake fluid irritates and damages paint.
Brake dust is treated as hazardous and never blown off.
Waste must be collected and disposed of properly.
examples: A learner wipes a drop of brake fluid off a fender with a dry cloth, which spreads it and damages the paint. Water and prompt cleaning would have been better.
A technician blows dust off a drum with an air gun and fills the workshop with dust. An enclosed brake washer would have prevented exposure.
A vehicle is raised with only a jack and a wheel is removed. The vehicle shifts. Jack stands and chocks would have prevented it.
safety: Do not start a task if you do not have the correct protective equipment.
If you are unsure about any step, stop and ask a qualified supervisor.
practice: Complete the Workshop Safety Checklist for a workspace of your choice and note anything that needs improvement.
Find the nearest approved collection point for used automotive fluids in your area.

check.q: Why should compressed air not be used on brake parts?
check.a: It puts hazardous dust into the air where it can be breathed.

check.q: What should you use to support a raised vehicle?
check.a: Jack stands placed at approved support points.

check.q: What should you do if brake fluid touches your skin?
Why should brake fluid containers be kept closed?
check.a: Most brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air.

check.q: How should used brake fluid be disposed of?
check.a: In a labelled, sealed container and through an approved collection according to local rules.

summary: Lift, support and chock vehicles correctly.
Treat dust and fluid as hazards.
Keep the workshop clean and dispose of waste responsibly.
